report:
Based on my research, the evidence actually **supports** the claim that opening a bedroom window improves sleep quality — contrary to your suspicion. Here's what the studies show:

**Key findings:**

- A Danish field intervention study (DTU, 2023) found that opening the bedroom window significantly improved air quality and sleep. 87% of participants reported sleeping soundly with the window open, compared to 70% with it closed. CO₂ levels dropped, and participants performed better cognitively the next day. ([DTU News](https://www.dtu.dk/english/newsarchive/2023/05/ventilate-your-bedroom-at-night-you-perform-better-the-next-day), [EurekAlert](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/988687))

- A 2024 review of 17 studies (2020–2024) consistently found that CO₂ levels above 1,000 ppm degrade sleep quality; ideally below 800 ppm. Opening windows is one effective way to reduce CO₂ buildup from sleeping occupants. ([Enventil/ASHRAE summary](https://www.enventil.com/blog-ashrae-bedroom-co2.html))

- A controlled experiment published in *Building and Environment* tested three CO₂ levels (750, 1,000, 1,300 ppm) and found that higher CO₂ reduced sleep depth, efficiency, and increased awakenings. ([ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132323011459))

- A 2025 international study confirmed that current minimum residential ventilation standards may be too low for bedrooms, resulting in disturbed sleep. ([Waseda University](https://www.waseda.jp/top/en/news/86065))

**One nuance:** Opening the bedroom *door* alone may not improve air quality sufficiently, since air from other rooms isn't necessarily fresh. The window is the more effective intervention. ([EurekAlert](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/988687))

**Conclusion:** The claim appears to be **true** — multiple peer-reviewed studies consistently show that opening a bedroom window improves sleep quality by reducing CO₂ and improving ventilation. You may want to reconsider your position.
